issues.failure_explanation: In the chain (eq:sumeij) the row sums of E are bounded by (b−a)/2·(1/2+Si(π)/π)·h·Σ_{j∈Z} g(jh) with g(s)=(π/2)cosh s/cosh²((π/2)sinh s), and this trapezoidal sum is then replaced by ∫g = 2 with a '≃' sign, not an inequality. No bound on h·Σ_j g(jh) is established anywhere, and the sum is not bounded by the integral in general (e.g. h·Σ_j g(jh) ≈ 2.03 at h = 1 and ≈ 3.14 at h = 2, versus ∫g = 2), while Theorem 3.2 is stated with no restriction on h. Hence the inequality (eq:Ebound), (eq:ImEinvNorm), and the bound (eq:MGSNorm2) asserted in Theorem 3.2 are not proved as written; the necessary nontrivial step of controlling the quadrature error of the DE weight is missing (the sign and size of the excess of the sum over the integral are never controlled).
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Insert a rigorous estimate of h·Σ_j g(jh) — e.g. prove g is even and decreasing on [0,∞) and compare the sum with the integral via a right-endpoint/midpoint argument, or use Poisson summation — showing h·Σ_j g(jh) ≤ 2+δ with (1/2+Si(π)/π)(1+δ/2) ≤ 1.1 (restricting h, equivalently N, if needed), or slightly weaken the constant 1.1 and the hypothesis 1.1L(b−a)<1. The theorem's form, rate, and the examples' conclusions are preserved.
issues.overall_effect: The constant 1.1 in Theorem 3.2's bound and in its hypothesis 1.1L(b−a)<1 is unsupported, so the theorem's quantitative guarantee, the sample estimate (eq:MGSboundsample), the condition checks in Examples 1–2, and the estimate w ≲ 1.1(b−a) all rest on an uncontrolled approximation. Theorem 3.1 (global convergence) is unaffected.
issues.title: Uncontrolled '≃' trapezoidal-sum step in the proof of Theorem 3.2's ‖E‖∞ ≤ 1.1(b−a)
issues.why_classification: Keeping the stated constant 1.1 requires a contained but genuinely nontrivial estimate of the trapezoidal sum (a new small lemma), or a limited weakening of the constant/hypothesis; no global proof architecture or major loss is involved, so it is moderate rather than serious, but it exceeds a routine local fix.

issues.failure_explanation: The step Σ_{k=1}^{N−i} 1/k ≤ 1+log(N−i) is valid only for N−i ≥ 1. At i = N the preceding sum Σ_{j=i+1}^N is empty and the row sum of |D|+|F| is the single positive term |w_NN|, but the displayed bound (1/2)+(1/π²)(1+log(N−i)) contains log 0 and is undefined (formally −∞), so the displayed chain (eq:dpfbound2), which feeds (eq:DpFNorm2) and Theorem 3.2 and is quantified there over i = −N,…,N, is false/ill-defined as written at the boundary index i = N.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Handle i = N separately (the row sum reduces to the diagonal term |w_NN| ≤ (b−a)(π/8)h, which is below the final bound), or replace log(N−i) by log max(N−i, 1); no other change is needed.
issues.overall_effect: Only the derivation of (eq:DpFNorm2) at the single boundary index i = N is defective; the final bound itself remains true there (|w_NN| is trivially below the final expression), so Theorem 3.2's conclusion is not endangered.
issues.title: log(N−i) bound in the |D|+|F| row-sum estimate is ill-defined at the boundary i = N
issues.why_classification: A local degenerate-case repair at one index value; the method, conclusion, rate, and advertised scope all survive unchanged.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: the constant $M$ can be chosen so that $w\le \frac{\rho}{M}$.

Thus, we can apply Theorem \ref{Th3-2} with $h=\log N/N$ and obtain the bound $\|M_{\rm GS}\|_{\infty}<1$ for $N\ge 2$. Hence, convergence of the Gauss-Seidel type iteration is guaranteed by Theorem \ref{Th3-1}.

issues.failure_explanation: With ρ = 1 and M = 2, condition (iii) requires w ≤ 1/2 exactly. The paper supports this only by the uncontrolled approximation w ≃ b−a = 1/2; its own estimates give at best w ≤ ‖E‖∞+‖D+F‖∞ ≤ 1.1(b−a)+… > 1/2, so w ≤ 1/2 is never established. The row sums of |(w_ij)| actually approach b−a = 1/2 (they are a trapezoidal sum of the DE weight, whose quadrature error has uncontrolled sign, plus nonnegative |D|+|F| corrections), so the claimed inequality holds, if at all, with vanishing margin and cannot be concluded from anything in the source. Hence the asserted satisfaction of Assumption 3.1, the applicability of Theorems 3.1/3.2 to Example 1, and the claim that convergence 'is guaranteed by Theorem 3.1' are unsupported as written.

issues.overall_effect: The formal basis for applying the paper's theorems to Example 1 is unreliable; the numerical observations and the theorems themselves are unaffected.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: In this section, we present some numerical examples that confirm the validity of Theorems \ref{Th3-1} and \ref{Th3-2}.
We also investigate the actual value of $\|M_{\rm GS}\|_{\infty}$ as a function of $N$ and compare it with the bound \eqref{eq:MGSNorm2}.
In this case, if we choose $\rho=1/2$, $\mathcal{D}_{\rm rho}^{\prime}$ implies $x_1\in[3/2,5/2]$, $x_2\in[0,1]$ and $x_3\in[1,2]$.

issues.failure_explanation: For Example 3, b−a = 1. Any Lipschitz constant valid on D_ρ satisfies L ≥ ‖J(x_a)‖∞ = 2.5 (the Jacobian row (x₂, x₁, 0) at x_a = (2, 1/2, 3/2) sums to 2.5), so 1.1L(b−a) ≥ 2.75 > 1: Theorem 3.2's hypothesis fails, and the bound formula (eq:MGSNorm2) then has a negative denominator, giving a negative value that cannot upper-bound ‖M_GS‖∞ ≥ 0. Moreover Assumption 3.1(iii) fails for every ρ > 0: it would require M ≤ ρ/w with w ≃ b−a = 1 (the paper's own estimate), but max_{D_ρ}‖f‖∞ ≥ (2+ρ)(1/2+ρ) > ρ for all ρ. Hence Assumption 3.1 cannot hold and neither Theorem 3.1 nor Theorem 3.2 applies to Example 3; the section's claim that the examples 'confirm the validity of Theorems 3.1 and 3.2', and Fig. Ex3-2's 'upper bound' (announced as the bound (eq:MGSNorm2)), are unsupported. The paper never verifies Assumption 3.1 for this example.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: For general $m$ and $A(0)$, the matrix exponential $\exp(tA(0))$ has to be calculated numerically.
Obtain $\{q_k(t)\}_{k=1}^m$ and $\{e_k(t)\}_{k=1}^{m-1}$ as the diagonal elements and the lower subdiagonal elements of $A(t)$, respectively.

issues.failure_explanation: For m ≥ 3 the LR factors of exp(tA(0)) are full triangular matrices in general, so the asserted structure does not exist. Concretely, for the symmetric tridiagonal A₀ with zero diagonal and unit off-diagonals, (exp(tA₀))₁₃ = t²/2 + O(t⁴) ≠ 0; since the first row of R_t equals the first row of exp(tA₀), r₁₃ ≠ 0, so R_t is not upper bidiagonal, and similarly ℓ₃₁ ≠ 0, so L_t is not merely subdiagonal. The description fits only the paper's m = 2 example, where 2×2 triangular factors are automatically bidiagonal. Taken literally, step (ii) is not executable for m ≥ 3 (no such decomposition exists), contradicting the advertised general-m applicability; with full triangular factors the construction is the classical Kostant/Symes solution of the Toda IVP, and the paper's m = 2 computation and the Lotka–Volterra solution used in Example 3 are correct.

failure_location.quote: Compute $\exp(tA(0))$ and its $LR$ decomposition $\exp(tA(0))=L_t R_t$, where $L_t$ is a unit lower subdiagonal matrix and $R_t$ is an upper bidiagonal matrix.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Correct step (ii) to state that L_t is unit lower triangular and R_t is upper triangular (the classical factorization), noting the standard hypotheses under which A(t) = L_t^{-1}A(0)L_t remains tridiagonal and solves (eq:Toda).
issues.overall_effect: The stated procedure for solving the Toda lattice IVP is mis-specified for m ≥ 3; a reader following it for general m (as the paper suggests) cannot carry out step (ii). No labelled result and no downstream computation in the paper (in particular Lemma B-1 and the Example 3 reference solution) is affected.
issues.title: Toda solution procedure asserts bidiagonal LR factors of exp(tA(0)), which do not exist for m ≥ 3
issues.why_classification: A local correction of the factor-structure description; the underlying construction, the m = 2 computation, and all downstream results remain valid.
